blocks.text: Imagine a circuit that can add two binary numbers or choose between multiple inputs based on a control signal. These are examples of combinational circuits, where the output depends solely on the current input.

blocks.markdown: Combinational circuits are fundamental components in digital systems. They are circuits whose outputs depend only on the current inputs, not on past inputs. This unit will explore three key types of combinational circuits: adders, multiplexers, and decoders.

blocks.title: Combinational Circuit
blocks.text: A circuit whose output is determined solely by its current inputs, without any memory of past inputs.

blocks.markdown:
### Adders
Adders are circuits that perform binary addition. We will look at two types: the half adder and the full adder.

blocks.title: Half Adder
blocks.text: A circuit that adds two single binary digits and produces a sum and a carry output.

blocks.latex: S = A \oplus B \quad \text{(Sum)} \quad C = A \cdot B \quad \text{(Carry)}
blocks.caption: Half Adder Equations

blocks.title: Designing a Half Adder
blocks.prompt: Design a half adder using basic logic gates.

steps.text: Identify the required outputs: Sum (S) and Carry (C).
Express the Sum as an XOR operation: $S = A \oplus B$.
Express the Carry as an AND operation: $C = A \cdot B$.
Construct the circuit using an XOR gate for the Sum and an AND gate for the Carry.

blocks.answer: The half adder is constructed using one XOR gate and one AND gate.

blocks.title: Full Adder
blocks.text: A circuit that adds three binary digits (two significant bits and a carry-in) and produces a sum and a carry-out.

blocks.latex: S = A \oplus B \oplus C_{in} \quad \text{(Sum)} \quad C_{out} = (A \cdot B) + (B \cdot C_{in}) + (A \cdot C_{in}) \quad \text{(Carry-out)}
blocks.caption: Full Adder Equations

blocks.title: Designing a Full Adder
blocks.prompt: Design a full adder using two half adders and an OR gate.

steps.text: Use the first half adder to add $A$ and $B$. This gives $S_1 = A \oplus B$ and $C_1 = A \cdot B$.
Use the second half adder to add $S_1$ and $C_{in}$. This gives $S = S_1 \oplus C_{in}$ and $C_2 = S_1 \cdot C_{in}$.
The final carry-out $C_{out}$ is the OR of $C_1$ and $C_2$: $C_{out} = C_1 + C_2$.

blocks.answer: The full adder is constructed using two half adders and one OR gate.

blocks.markdown:
### Multiplexers
A multiplexer (MUX) is a device that selects one of several input signals and forwards the selected input to a single output line.

blocks.title: Multiplexer
blocks.text: A circuit that selects one of many inputs and forwards it to the output, based on control signals.

blocks.markdown:
### Decoders
A decoder is a circuit that converts binary information from $n$ input lines to a maximum of $2^n$ unique output lines.

blocks.title: Decoder
blocks.text: A circuit that decodes a binary input into a one-hot output, where only one output line is high for any given input.

rows: Sum: $A \oplus B \oplus C_{in}$, Carry-out: $(A \cdot B) + (B \cdot C_{in}) + (A \cdot C_{in})$
blocks.caption: Comparison of Combinational Circuits

blocks.markdown:
### Propagation Delay
Propagation delay is the time taken for an input change to affect the output. It is crucial in determining the speed of a combinational circuit.

blocks.title: Propagation Delay
blocks.text: The total delay of a combinational circuit is the sum of the delays of the individual gates along the longest path from input to output.

points: Combinational circuits include adders, multiplexers, and decoders.
Adders perform binary addition, multiplexers select inputs, and decoders convert binary inputs to unique outputs.
Propagation delay affects the speed of combinational circuits.
